plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to plan, rehearse and deliver a 3-minute talk to a small group, with one clear point, a steady opening, and a close you don't trail off from.
plan.horizon14: Later: a 10-minute talk with slides that help you instead of replacing you.
plan.horizon28: Later: handle live questions and speak without notes to a room of 30 or more.

picture.name: Taking someone on a walk
picture.line: A talk is a walk you lead: you pick one destination, you know the route, you set the pace, and the people with you only need to follow one step at a time.

chapters.title: Pick one destination
chapters.covers: Why every talk needs exactly one point, and how to write that point as a single 15-word sentence before you write anything else.
chapters.outcome: You can write the one sentence your talk exists to deliver, and say it out loud in under 10 seconds.
chapters.hook: Most talks fail before a word is spoken: the speaker can't say what the point is.

chapters.title: Know who's walking with you
chapters.covers: What your listeners already know, what they care about, and how that changes what you leave out.
chapters.outcome: You can describe your audience in 3 lines and cut any part of your talk they don't need.
chapters.hook: What your listeners already know decides what you cut. Most speakers cut nothing.

chapters.title: Plan the route
chapters.covers: The 3-part shape of a short talk: say where you're going, go there in 3 steps, say where you've arrived.
chapters.outcome: You can lay out a 3-minute talk on one index card with an opening line, 3 steps and a closing line.
chapters.hook: Why do you remember three things from a good talk and nothing from a bad one?

chapters.title: Start walking without stumbling
chapters.covers: Your first 20 seconds: a planned first sentence, a pause before you speak, and the 2 or 3 things to do with your hands and feet.
chapters.outcome: You can open a talk from memory with a sentence that names the destination, and stand still while you do it.
chapters.hook: The first line is the only line worth memorising word for word. Here's why.

chapters.title: Set the pace
chapters.covers: Speaking slower than feels natural, pausing at full stops, and dropping filler like 'um' and 'so' by replacing them with silence.
chapters.outcome: You can record yourself for 1 minute, count your fillers, and halve them on a second take.
chapters.hook: A 3-second pause feels like an hour to you and like confidence to them.

chapters.title: When your legs shake
chapters.covers: What nerves do to your body (fast breath, dry mouth, racing speech) and 3 physical things to do in the 2 minutes before you start.
chapters.outcome: You can name what your nerves do to you and use a breathing pattern to slow your heart before you stand up.
chapters.hook: The shaking never fully goes away. Experienced speakers just stop waiting for it to.

chapters.title: Arrive, then stop
chapters.covers: Rehearsing out loud 3 times, closing on your one sentence instead of 'so, yeah, that's it', and delivering the full talk to 2 or more people.
chapters.outcome: You can deliver your 3-minute talk to a small group, end on your one sentence, and stop.
chapters.hook: Reading your notes silently is not rehearsal. Your mouth has never said the words.

sources.what: TED Talks: The Official TED Guide to Public Speaking
sources.why: the idea that a talk carries one throughline and everything else serves it
the shape of a talk as a journey the audience takes, not a list the speaker reads

sources.who: Dale Carnegie and J. Berg Esenwein
sources.why: nerves as normal and rehearsal out loud as the cure
